This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place.
In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior.

Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily find and exploit. The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with Theorem, however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level. While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite trillions of test runs. As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development.

METASTONE, an independent compute operator, has introduced TokenFleet, a distributed scheduling framework for large language model inference. The company announced it during the 2026 CCF National High Performance Computing Conference.
TokenFleet does not make individual models run faster. Instead it targets cluster-level problems: requests piling up on some GPU instances while capacity sits idle elsewhere, long-document jobs crowding out real-time chat, and timeouts or cancellations that burn compute without producing a usable answer. METASTONE frames the goal as raising effective token output, meaning tokens from requests that finish successfully and meet their service targets.
The framework has three parts. TokenPilot picks an instance inside a model pool. It weighs the gain from reusing a cached prompt prefix, which skips repeated prefill computation, against the cost of waiting in a longer queue on that instance. It estimates workload from input size, output budget and reusable prefix, then scores candidates using queue depth, in-flight tokens, KV cache pressure and predicted latency.
FleetMind handles routing across data centers. It tracks which sites actually have the right model version deployed and ready, along with live capacity and network conditions, then sends new requests to another site only when permissions and data-residency rules allow it and the cost comparison favors it.

AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).
Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.
Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”
“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”
Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains.

Shenzhen-based chip designer Lanxin Computing has launched what it calls a converged-computing supernode, extending its RISC-V AI inference platform from a single chip and server to a cluster-level system. The company presented the product at the 2026 RISC-V China Summit, where chief technology officer Jia Xinxia gave a keynote on the LX500 processor that underpins it.
The idea behind the design is to cut down on data movement. In a conventional inference server, a CPU and a separate accelerator card each have their own memory, and model weights, activations and context data shuttle between them over PCIe. Lanxin's approach integrates general-purpose computing and AI computing on the same chip and lets both share a unified memory pool, which the company says helps with time to first token, prefill and long-context workloads.
According to the company, LX500 packs 48 RISC-V CPU cores, split into 32 performance cores and 16 efficiency cores, alongside AI vector and matrix engines rated at 75 TOPS of INT8 compute. It supports precisions from INT4 to FP32, shares DDR5 memory across the chip, and supports CXL memory expansion. Earlier company materials say the chip follows the RVA23 profile and the RVV 1.0 vector extension.

Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers.
More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to.
That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI.
But the problem, she told TechCrunch, is simply that AI is developing faster than companies can adapt. “AI works very well for [managers] individually, but they also have a different role as managers. They need to drive the organization as well … Their struggle is [due to] the fact that AI is just moving faster than the organizational processes,” Levi said.

be involved and consulted by AI when it comes to crucial tasks and decisions.

Retraining workers is the most popular policy option for mitigating labor market disruption from AI. In this report, the authors investigate whether these programs would work in the face of significant labor market disruption.
The review is part of our Economic Research team's work on AI's effects on the economy. Our Economic Index tracks how AI is being used across occupations and industries. Earlier this year, we published a framework for measuring AI's effects on the labor market and identifying the jobs most likely to be affected. Our Economic Policy Framework sets out possible policy responses, including worker retraining, across a range of scenarios. We want to understand the evidence behind each of these policy responses.
The review draws on 56 randomized US studies, combined in a new meta-analysis, along with experimental evidence from Europe. On average, job training programs produce positive but modest effects: for each person offered a training slot, employment rises by two to three percentage points and earnings by roughly $1,000 a year, against a cost of about $13,000. GPU applications are processing ever-growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators. According to the 2025 Stanford AI Index, compute for notable AI models has been doubling approximately every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling approximately every eight months. As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory. This avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system. GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors.
At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development. As of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python while the main application interface to GDS is the cuFile C API.
NVIDIA KvikIO, a Python and C++ library for high-performance file I/O, bridges this gap. It provides high-level, idiomatic Python and C++ interfaces, along with additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.

StartLux, the young Chinese team behind the StartLux-Decision model family, has open-sourced Prism, an inference engine written specifically for decision models. The code was released on GitHub on October 22, and the company describes it as the first openly available engine built for this class of model rather than adapted from a chat-oriented framework.
Decision models read material and return a judgment rather than long text: yes or no, an option choice, or a risk score with probabilities. StartLux-Decision v1.1, released on October 16, previously ran on a general framework based on vLLM. According to StartLux, engines such as vLLM and SGLang are designed for token-by-token generation, so every question becomes a separate request and the large output layer is computed in full each time.
Prism makes four changes. First, it narrows the output layer. For the 27B StartLux-Decision model, a general engine scores about 248,000 candidate tokens, while a decision task needs only the letters A to Z, so Prism cuts that computation to about 0.01 percent of the original. Second, it uses what the team calls forest-style batching: shared instructions form the root, shared reference material forms the trunk and each question is a branch, so common work runs only once. Third, matrix operations run in int8 with int32 accumulation, which makes results independent of batch size and scheduling order and keeps outputs bit-identical. Fourth, a mixed scheduler lets up to 64 longer reasoning requests share the GPU with direct-answer requests, with decoding steps precompiled as CUDA graphs so new

Abstract:Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. SIwithin
SIwithin runs an agent CLI unattended on a brief, inside a fence around the folders you give it and under a dollar budget, and tells you afterwards, in one ledger line, whether the run was done, finished, contract unmet, killed at its budget or timer, stopped by the CLI's own flag, or refused before it began, and what it cost by the proxy's count. done means the CLI finished and the brief's own test, when you give one (--done "<text>" present in the result, --absent "<text>" not), passed; a run that stopped is never written as done, and the exit status is 0 only when it was. It keeps three promises with a tool and not with hope:
The run touches only the folders it was given. Your home folder is refused, for reading and writing, and the run's folders are allowed back.
The run cannot spend more than the dollars it was given. A budget per run, a cap across all runs, a timer on every run, and, for the Claude adapter, a loopback proxy that is the one door to the API: the run holds a per-run token and not your key, and every request it makes, however it makes it, is metered there and refused past the budget. Where a CLI cannot be stopped mid-run, the tool refuses it unless you say you accept that (see "The ledger" and "The Codex adapter").
Every run leaves one line saying what it cost and whether it was done.
Why not the CLI's own budget flag? Claude Code's --max-budget-usd and turn limit are kept by the process you are trying to bound, which holds your key and can reach the API by any path it likes, a script or a second client included, and they say nothing about what t

Large language models (LLMs) used to program helpful robots could be exploited, new research shows
By adding trigger words to large language models (LLMs), researchers at Binghamton University demonstrated how a service robot designed to slice an apple could be reprogrammed to instead slice a person’s hand.
By John Brhel
October 20, 2026
share via facebook

Large language models (LLMs) like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google Gemini are increasingly being used to help robots perform tasks, but what if LLMs could be exploited to turn helpful robots into harmful robots?
A team of computer scientists at Binghamton University has demonstrated that hidden trigger words inserted maliciously into LLMs could cause a robot to go off-script and perform dangerous actions.
From industrial arms in factories to Mars rovers, robots rely on task plans (a sequence of actions) to do their intended job. Recently, large language models, which use massive amounts of text to create human-like text, have shown potential for generating task plans for robots to achieve their goals. Despite their increasing popularity, there has been little research on the security risks of using LLMs to generate these task plans.

AI video generation is no longer just about producing a visually impressive clip. For creators looking to use AI to make short films, advertisements or even feature films, the harder questions are whether characters can remain consistent, whether shots can unfold as intended, and whether a video can tell a coherent story from beginning to end.
Kling AI’s latest release, Kling 4.0, introduces features designed to tackle these challenges. The model update focuses on motion performance, creative control and longer-form storytelling.
Kling 4.0 supports native video generation of up to 30 seconds in a single generation, along with up to 15 multimodal reference assets and 10 keyframes, giving creators more control over characters, scenes, actions and camera movements. Rather than focusing solely on visual quality, these features reflect a broader effort to make AI video generation more consistent and easier to control.
Screenshot from videos generated by Kling 4.0
From generating images to directing shots
AI video creation has traditionally relied heavily on text prompts. Creators describe the scenes they want, and the model generates the footage. However, complex camera movements, character actions and scene transitions can be difficult to control precisely. Even when individual shots look convincing, combining them can result in inconsistent character appearances or discontinuous actions.
